document_sections.heading: 9. PENILE SIZE ABNORMALITIES AND DYSMORPHOPHOBIA
document_sections.content: This chapter addresses complaints about penile dimensions, anatomical causes of shortness, body-image concerns, assessment, and non-surgical and surgical management.

document_sections.heading: 9.1 Definition, epidemiology and classification
document_sections.content: Penile-size complaints encompass distinct anatomical, functional, and psychological conditions. Assessment must distinguish a genuinely small penis from reduced visibility of a normal-sized penis and from distress about normal dimensions.

document_sections.heading: 9.1.1 History
document_sections.content: Across cultures and historical periods, penile size has carried meanings connected with masculinity, fertility, sexual performance, and male identity. Phallic imagery and contemporary media, including pornography, reinforce these associations. Cosmetic procedures can improve body-related self-esteem, anxiety, social phobia, depressive mood, well-being, and quality of life (QoL), but candidates with psychopathology may experience adverse outcomes. In one real-life report, 84% of women were satisfied with their male partners’ penile size; among the men, 55% were satisfied and 45% wanted a larger penis. Men with greater social-desirability were more likely to report a larger penis. A cited study found that an average 15% reduction in penile length, producing shallower penetration, was associated with a statistically significant 18% reduction in overall sexual pleasure. Perceived penile size affects sexual functioning and QoL and affects sexual life in about 10% of men; the proportion is markedly higher among those seeking enlargement. Some men remain dissatisfied or emotionally poorly adjusted after augmentation, particularly when psychopathology is present, and invasive treatment may harm this vulnerable group. Clinicians should anticipate such vulnerability through individualised psychological assessment and consider cultural expectations. Increasing worldwide use of medical and surgical augmentation creates a need for evidence-based clinical guidance.

document_sections.heading: 9.1.2 Definition
document_sections.content: A complaint of a short penis presents diagnostic and therapeutic difficulties. Accurate shaft measurement is essential, but neither a standard normal size nor a universally accepted measurement approach has been established; the document points to Table S9.1 for published measurements. Observer differences and underestimation by stretched penile length (SPL) relative to erection complicate assessment. SPL runs from the pubic symphysis to the glans apex and most closely approximates erect length among the described measurements. Micropenis is defined here as SPL less than 2.5 standard deviations (SD) below the mean for age and race. The evidence summary distinguishes true micropenis, a complaint of shortness, and buried penis; excessive anxiety about a normal-sized penis is termed small penis anxiety/syndrome (LE 4). It describes true micropenis as congenital, associated with a genetic or endocrine cause, and a stretched length 2.5 SD cm below the population-group average (LE 3). Buried penis involves a normal-sized organ whose visible and functional length is reduced by pathology such as obesity or traumatic length loss, with prepubic, scrotal, or penile skin or subcutaneous tissue covering it (LE 3). Penile Dysmorphic Disorder denotes cases of Body Dysmorphic Disorder focused on a perceived defect in normal penile size or shape, with mental-health impairment and substantial disruption of important life areas (LE 3).

document_sections.heading: 9.1.3 Epidemiology and Classification
document_sections.content: The overall incidence of micropenis in males is uncertain; epidemiological reports identify it in 0.015% - 0.66% of male newborns. Possible increasing prevalence has prompted concern about exposure to endocrine-disrupting chemicals before and during pregnancy. Demand for augmentation remains substantial despite micropenis being uncommon; increased pornography exposure and distorted perceptions of normal dimensions may partly explain it. Table 9.1 groups adult conditions underlying shortness or dysmorphophobia by cause, definition, pathogenesis, and reported prevalence.

document_sections.heading: Table 9.1: Classification of the clinical conditions underlying a short penis condition or dysmorphophobia in adults
document_sections.content: The table distinguishes acquired false shortness caused by reduced shaft exposure despite normal dimensions; congenital intrinsic shortness associated with incomplete genital development; acquired intrinsic shortness caused by pathological shortening of the corpora cavernosa; and acquired body dysmorphic disorder involving a perceived appearance defect and substantial distress or impairment. It lists causes and prevalence estimates where available: 0.9 - 2.1 for congenital intrinsic shortness and 1.8 – 9.5 for body dysmorphic disorder, with prevalence marked NA for both false and acquired intrinsic shortness.

document_sections.heading: 9.1.3.1 False penile shortness - congenital or acquired
document_sections.content: Buried penis is the established cause of false penile shortness. In children, congenital concealment or webbing can result from atypical dartos-fascia development that traps the shaft in surrounding tissue. Adult acquired buried penis (AABP) is recognised as an acquired disorder. Chronic inflammation of the penile dartos is thought to produce progressive scarring and retraction of surrounding coverings. Entrapment creates moisture favourable to bacterial and fungal growth, perpetuating inflammation and fibrosis. AABP prevalence is unknown, although incidence appears to be rising alongside obesity, its principal risk factor. Other contributors include aggressive circumcision, surgery in people with obesity or penile cancer (PC), and chronic skin disease such as lichen sclerosis (LS). Erectile and voiding problems, difficulty maintaining genital hygiene, and poor QoL commonly accompany AABP. Table S9.2 details risks and issues that can require surgery. Treatment seeks to restore functional anatomy and improve QoL; proposed classifications use presentation and required operation.

document_sections.heading: 9.1.3.2 Intrinsic penile shortness – congenital
document_sections.content: This group includes true micropenis. Male genital malformations are described as the most common birth defects yet a rare clinical entity, with prevalence between 0.9% and 2.1%. Fetal and pubertal hormonal stimulation influence genital growth; genetic syndromes can disrupt the hormonal axis. Up to 25% of micropenis cases may be isolated without a definitive cause. Table 9.2 categorises associated causes. Bladder exstrophy–epispadias complex (BEEC) is the most studied associated condition and ranges from epispadias to bladder or cloacal exstrophy. Its birth prevalence is 1/10,000. Reconstruction aims to improve body image, but long-term psychosocial and psychosexual problems frequently persist. Male infertility is also frequent and is associated with impaired sperm quantity or quality and hormonal function.

document_sections.heading: Table 9.2: Classification of the clinical conditions underlying intrinsic penile shortness in adults
document_sections.content: The table lists hypogonadotropic hypogonadism associated with genetic disease or pituitary or hypothalamic injury; Hypergonadotropic Hypogonadism associated with chromosomal changes such as Klinefelter Syndrome, Androgen Synthesis Defects, or dysgenetic gonads; Syndromic or Multiple Congenital Anomalies, including bladder exstrophy–epispadias complex and hypospadias; and an unknown-cause category.

document_sections.heading: 9.1.3.3 Intrinsic penile shortness – acquired
document_sections.content: Acquired disorders can shorten the corpora cavernosa abruptly after trauma or surgical amputation for penile cancer, or gradually through corporal fibrosis. Traffic accidents and gunshot wounds commonly cause traumatic genital injury. Rarely, circumcision or operations such as hypospadias repair, penile prosthesis implantation, or urethroplasty cause amputation and reduced length. Common chronic causes include PD and prostate-cancer treatment, particularly radical prostatectomy (RP), as well as radical cystectomy. The text refers to Table 9.2 for acquired causes, although that table presents a different classification.

document_sections.heading: 9.1.3.4 Body dysmorphic disorder
document_sections.content: Under the American Psychiatric Association (APA; DSM-5) definition, Body dysmorphic disorder (BDD) involves marked distress over perceived appearance flaws that others cannot see or can see only slightly, together with substantial social or occupational impairment; it falls within Obsessive Compulsive and Related Disorders. Muscle dysmorphia is a BDD form involving preoccupation, usually in men, with perceived inadequate musculature or body shape. Penile Dysmorphic Disorder (PDD) is a shorthand for BDD centred on penile size or shape, not a separate APA DSM-5 code. Small penis anxiety (SPA), also called small penis syndrome, instead denotes excessive worry about a normal-sized penis; it is outside APA nomenclature, although affected men may be at risk of BDD. These definitions exclude true micropenis. Reported BDD prevalence is 2.2% of men in the USA and 1.8% in Germany. BDD is expected in 3%-16% of cosmetic-surgery patients, with rates of 15.3% in men and 10.9% in women. Distinguish these conditions from Gender Dysphoria, involving distress about mismatch between gender identity and assigned sex at birth, and Koro, involving sudden fear that the penis will retract into the abdomen.

document_sections.heading: 9.1.4 Summary of evidence and recommendations for classification
document_sections.content: The evidence summary calls male genital malformations rare, with overall prevalence between 0.9% and 2.1% (LE 3). It identifies obesity, lichen sclerosis, and penile-cancer treatment as AABP risks (LE 4); describes common erectile, voiding, hygiene, and QoL problems (LE 3); and notes that available AABP systems classify presentation and operative requirements (LE 3). It links BEEC to genital malformations, especially micropenis (LE 2b), identifies traumatic or cancer-related surgical amputation as the commonest acute causes of intrinsic shortening (LE 3), and lists PD, prostate-cancer treatments including RP, radiation therapy and androgen-deprivation therapy, and radical cystectomy as the most frequent chronic causes (LE 2b). BDD entails substantial distress or impairment (LE 2b); PDD is shorthand for BDD focused on penile dimensions or shape (LE 4); and BDD/PDD may be identified among cosmetic-surgery applicants (LE 3). Recommendations: thoroughly examine the genitals of all men, particularly those with BMI > 30, lichen sclerosis, or prior penile cancer plus urinary or sexual complaints or poor cosmetic appearance, to rule out AABP (Strong). Classify AABP presentation and operative management with classification systems (Weak). Ask about BDD/PDD when someone with normal penile dimensions reports shortness (Strong).

document_sections.heading: 9.2 Diagnosis
document_sections.content: Evaluation combines medical and sexual history, genital examination and measurement, and assessment of psychological concerns. Imaging lacks evidence supporting routine use for a complaint of penile shortness.

document_sections.heading: 9.2.1 Medical history, physical examination and psychological assessment
document_sections.content: Assessment should establish possible anatomical and acquired causes, document sexual function and expectations, measure penile dimensions and shape, and recognise psychological vulnerability before treatment decisions.

document_sections.heading: 9.2.1.1 Medical History
document_sections.content: Begin assessment of perceived shortness with a detailed medical history. Investigate phimosis, priapism, hypospadias or epispadias, penile injury, penile or prostate cancer, and penile pain with or without acquired curvature suggestive of PD. Record any current or previous BDD diagnosis.

document_sections.heading: 9.2.1.2 Sexual history
document_sections.content: Use open-ended discussion of sexual education, development, experiences, and fantasies. Potential psychometric measures include The International Index of Erectile Function [IIEF] for function, The Sexual Distress Scale for men for distress, and Global Measure of Sexual Satisfaction for satisfaction. Sexual Inhibition/ Sexual Excitation Scales may assess excitation and inhibition, while Global Measure of Relationship Satisfaction may assess relationships. Pay particular attention to performance expectations, for example through The Dysfunctional Sexual Beliefs Questionnaire; The Body-Image Questionnaire may supplement assessment of body image.

document_sections.heading: 9.2.1.3 Physical examination and penile size measurements
document_sections.content: Initial examination should focus closely on the genitals. Length and shape measurement is required before planning medical or surgical care, although surgeons use differing methods. The EAU Guidelines Panel on Sexual and Reproductive Health regards stretched penile length as the minimum measurement and favours additional flaccid and erect measurements after intracavernosal erectogenic injection when feasible; these additional measurements are compulsory before surgical indication. Measure stretched length dorsally and/or ventrally from the penopubic skin junction to the glans tip (STT), or dorsally from pubic bone to glans tip (BTT), using a tape or Vernier calliper. Published assessment and reporting methods remain heterogeneous, preventing measurement standardisation or consensus on normal size. Document girth in every patient, including distal coronal and mid-shaft circumference; these measurements and the head-to-base ratio inform shape assessment, which photography can document. STT underestimates erect length by about 20%, whereas BTT correlates more closely with erect length, especially in overweight or obese men. Table 9.3 outlines measurement states and anatomical sites.

document_sections.heading: Table 9.3: Penile size measurement
document_sections.content: The table specifies erect, stretched, and flaccid states and skin-junction or pubic-bone landmarks for length; erect or flaccid states and proximal, middle-shaft, and distal sites for girth; and the head-to-base ratio and standardised photography for shape.

document_sections.heading: 9.2.1.4 Psychological assessment
document_sections.content: Some men requesting augmentation, usually an operation, have substantial psychological vulnerability including BDD; they may experience worsening psychopathology or suicide attempts and are unlikely to obtain the results they expect. Freely available self-report screens include the Body Dysmorphic Disorder Questionnaire and The Cosmetic Procedure Screening Scale for Penile Dysmorphic Disorder for body- or penis-focused dysmorphia; The Male Genital Self-Image Scale and the Index of Male Genital Image for genital perceptions and satisfaction; and the Beliefs About Penile Size Scale for size beliefs and internal psychological processes. An accredited mental-health expert should evaluate BDD/PDD, other psychopathology, and differentiation from personality, obsessivecompulsive, psychotic, and emotional-spectrum disorders. Assess subjective perception of penile size as well.

document_sections.heading: 9.2.1.5 Counselling and outcomes assessment - Validated questionnaires
document_sections.content: The Augmentation Phalloplasty Patient Selection and Satisfaction Inventory (APPSSI) is a 5-item instrument proposed for surgical selection and counselling; Beliefs about Penis Size (BAPS) is a 10-item instrument designed for audit and outcomes research on penile-size beliefs. Neither correlated with measured size, and lack of objective validation limits their application. IIEF-15 and Male Sexual Health Questionnaire (MSHQ) can record baseline sexual function and subsequent change; Erectile Dysfunction Inventory of Treatment Satisfaction (EDITS) can help evaluate satisfaction of patients and partners.

document_sections.heading: 9.2.2 Imaging
document_sections.content: Evidence on imaging in patients concerned about penile shortness is insufficient. Penile Doppler ultrasound or magnetic resonance imaging may add anatomical information about burial, but evidence does not establish an advantage over examination sufficient to warrant routine use. The evidence summary rates medical and sexual history plus examination as essential (LE 4); STT underestimation and the stronger erect-length correlation of BTT, especially with overweight or obesity, at LE 2b; additional flaccid and erect measurements and girth assessment at LE 4; named self-report psychopathology screens and mental-health counselling for vulnerable augmentation candidates at LE 2b; and questionnaires such as APPSSI, BAPS, IIEF-15, MSHQ, and EDITS for baseline function and size beliefs at LE 4. Recommendations: obtain comprehensive medical and sexual histories for every shortness complaint (Strong); use stretched STT or BTT to define length (Weak); obtain flaccid and erect length measurements (Weak); measure girth in every patient reporting shortness (Weak); screen for BDD with validated questionnaires when penile size is normal (Weak); use validated measures such as IIEF-15 and BAPS for baseline sexual function and size beliefs (Weak); and refer suspected BDD for mental-health counselling (Strong).

document_sections.heading: 9.3 Management
document_sections.content: Management includes psychological care, non-invasive approaches, endocrine treatment in selected boys, and operations chosen according to the underlying condition. Benefits, limitations, psychological suitability, and complications differ by intervention.

document_sections.heading: 9.3.1 Non-surgical Treatments
document_sections.content: The non-surgical approaches discussed are psychotherapy, penile traction therapy, vacuum erection devices, and endocrinological treatment. Their indications and evidence differ.

document_sections.heading: 9.3.1.1 Psychotherapy
document_sections.content: Requests for augmentation often seek improved self-image and self-esteem, and cosmetic treatment may improve emotional well-being and QoL. Psychotherapy is recommended when psychopathological comorbidity or harmful relationship dynamics contribute to the request, not as a way of obstructing a legitimate choice. Exploring patient and partner motivations and expectations appears important, although no other empirical evidence for this target is described. Men with BDD or SPA may perceive a pronounced gap between actual and ideal penile dimensions and believe a larger penis is necessary. Cognitive behaviour therapy for BDD could be applied to penile-size anxiety, but clinical trials have not been reported. Therapy should communicate normal variation in genital size and form; expectation management may improve well-being and the surgical experience.

document_sections.heading: 9.3.1.2 Penile traction therapy
document_sections.content: Penile traction therapy (PTT) offers a non-invasive means of increasing length. In a prospective pilot phase-II study, Gontero et al. prescribed a penile extender for at least 4 hours/day for 6 months and found length gains of +2.3 cm flaccid and +1.7 cm stretched (both p < 0.001), without significant girth change. In another prospective study, Nikoobakht et al. found mean flaccid length rising from 8.8 ± 1.2 cm to 10.5 ± 1.2 cm (P < 0.05) and stretched length from 11.5 ± 1.0 cm to 13.2 ± 1.4 cm (p < 0.05) after 3 months of device use. A reported 6-month comparison with baseline gave gains of +1.7 ± 0.8, +1.3 ± 0.4, and +1.2 ± 0.4 cm for flaccid, stretched, and erect lengths, respectively (p < 0.001, for all). Table 9.4 compares available studies and their protocols and outcomes. Overall, PTT appears to increase flaccid and stretched length with few side effects, but not girth. Confidence is limited by absent RCTs and small, heterogeneous cohorts. PTT has also been reported effective for length restoration or deformity correction associated with PD or post-RP conditions.

document_sections.heading: Table 9.4: Penile traction therapy (PPT)
document_sections.content: This table presents prospective studies by Nowroozi et al., Nikoobakht et al., and Gontero et al., with participant numbers of 54, 23, and 21, respectively. It compares devices, schedules, mean ages, and changes in flaccid, stretched, erect, or circumference measurements; one circumference outcome is NR.

document_sections.heading: 9.3.1.3 Vacuum erection device
document_sections.content: Vacuum erection devises (VED) are generally considered after failure of oral ED treatment, but evidence for lengthening is sparse. In a study of 27 men with SPL < 10 cm, VED use three times a week for 20 minutes per occasion over 6 months produced no significant increase in flaccid or stretched length. The document separately reports benefits after PPI and RP.

document_sections.heading: 9.3.1.4 Endocrinological therapies
document_sections.content: Testosterone has long been administered to infants or prepubertal boys with micropenis to promote penile growth. Topical T or DHT has also been proposed; reported results favour DHT, especially after poor response to T or with type 2 alpha reductase deficiency. Combined hCG and FSH has been proposed with favourable reported outcomes. Direct comparisons between the suggested treatments are unavailable.

document_sections.heading: 9.3.1.5 Summary of evidence and recommendations for the non-surgical management of short penile size
document_sections.content: The evidence summary supports psychotherapy when psychopathology or harmful relationship dynamics contribute to augmentation requests, while rejecting its use to prevent legitimate personal choice (LE 3). Cognitive behaviour therapy for BDD could be applied to penile-size anxiety (LE 3). PTT achieves lengthening (LE 3), whereas VEDs have proved ineffective for that purpose (LE 3). Testosterone therapy, transdermal dihydrotestosterone, and recombinant gonadotropins can restore size in boys with micropenis or disorders of sex development (LE 2b); testosterone does not increase size in adult men or those with late-onset hypogonadism (LE 3). Recommendations: consider psychotherapy for relevant psychopathology or harmful relationship dynamics (Strong); consider PTT for conservative lengthening (Weak); consider VEDs for lengthening (Weak), despite the contrary evidence summary; use endocrinological treatment to restore size in boys with micropenis or disorders of sex development (Strong); and do not use testosterone or other hormonal therapies for enlargement after puberty (Strong).

document_sections.heading: 9.3.2 Surgical Treatments
document_sections.content: The surgical discussion separates reconstruction for AABP, congenital and acquired intrinsic shortness, and procedures intended to increase circumference.

document_sections.heading: 9.3.2.1 Surgical treatment of adult acquired buried penis
document_sections.content: AABP operations seek to expose the shaft and restore functional genital anatomy. Procedure selection depends on anatomy and complexity, and counselling must account for postoperative complications.

document_sections.heading: 9.3.2.1.1 Adult acquired buried penis surgical procedures classification
document_sections.content: Under the classification proposed by Pariser et al., lower-complexity procedures include shaft exposure, coverage with flaps or grafts, and scrotal reconstruction; more complex options include excision of suprapubic fat (escutcheonectomy) or abdominal-wall skin and fat (apronectomy). Surgery aims to release the trapped shaft, reconstruct its coverings, and, where appropriate, remove adjacent or excess abdominal tissue to limit recurrence while improving QoL and minimising harm. Encourage lifestyle and risk-factor changes, particularly weight reduction, before surgery to reduce complications. Tables S9.3 and S9.4 summarise interventions and outcomes. The document twice reports effective treatment, low recurrence, and satisfactory function alongside substantial postoperative morbidity, including up to 3.5% of grade V according to ClavienDindo Classification in one passage and up to 3.5% of grade V according to Clavien-Dindo Classification in another; the latter passage points to Table 26. The evidence summary says multiple procedures can restore anatomy (LE 3), postoperative complications are substantial (LE 3), lifestyle change and especially weight loss can proactively reduce surgical risk (LE 4), and function may improve with low recurrence (LE 3). Recommendations: discuss benefits and complications extensively (Strong); begin lifestyle and risk-factor modification, particularly weight loss, to reduce complications and optimise outcomes (Strong); and consider surgery for AABP (Weak).

document_sections.heading: 9.3.2.2 Surgical treatment of congenital intrinsic penile shortness
document_sections.content: Described operations span relatively limited interventions such as suspensory ligament release (SLR) to extensive reconstruction such as total phallic reconstruction (TPR). Choice must take procedural complexity and potential complications into account.

document_sections.heading: 9.3.2.2.1 Suspensory ligament release
document_sections.content: SLR divides the penile suspensory ligament through an infrapubic approach and can be paired with elongating V-Y skin plasty; Table S9.5 summarises reported outcomes. Littara et al. treated 21 patients with lengthening, 33 with enlargement, and 301 with both using lipofilling, V-Y infrapubic plasty, and SLR. At 12 months, resting length rose significantly from 8.8 cm to 11.4 cm, SPL from 12.4 cm to 13.5 cm, and resting circumference from 8.3 cm to 11.06 cm; IIEF-5 rose from 21.5 to 23.

document_sections.heading: 9.3.2.2.2 Ventral phalloplasty/scrotoplasty
document_sections.content: Ventral shaft skin plasty shifts the penoscrotal angle proximally to reveal more shaft. Xu et al. used a longitudinal incision or Z-plasty at the junction and fixation of tunica albuginea to proximal tunica dartos in 41 patients. All had successful correction, with median flaccid-length improvement of +2.1 cm.

document_sections.heading: 9.3.2.2.3 Suprapubic lipoplasty/liposuction/lipectomy
document_sections.content: Reducing the suprapubic fat pad through liposuction or surgical lipectomy exposes more shaft. Ghanem et al. treated ten patients using a 50-cc syringe and 3- and 6-mm needles; fat removal ranged from 325 to 850 mL, with a mean of 495.50 ± 155.39 mL. Satisfaction was very high in three (30%), satisfactory in five (50%), neutral in one (10%), and negative in one (10%); nobody was very dissatisfied. In 20 patients undergoing Shaeer’s monsplasty technique, visible flaccid length at 3 months was 7.1 ± 2.1cm, a 57.9% improvement, and visible erect length was 11.8 ± 2.1cm, a 32% improvement. At final follow-up (18 months), satisfaction rate had improved by 73.1%.

document_sections.heading: 9.3.2.2.4 Total phallic reconstruction
document_sections.content: TPR creates a new phallus and neo-urethra. Because potential benefit must be balanced against complications, it is reserved for severe insufficiency such as congenital micropenis or exstrophy-epispadias complex. Lumen et al. treated seven males aged 15 to 42 years, using 6 radial forearm free flaps and 1 anterolateral thigh flap; implant surgery was offered approximately 1 year later. No complication occurred during neophallus formation; two early postoperative complications and urinary stricture and/or fistula in two patients were reported. Satisfaction was high in six and moderate in one. Four received implants, of which 50% were later removed. In Perovic et al.’s 12-patient musculocutaneous latissimus dorsi (MLD) series, mean (range) follow-up was 31 (6–74) months; phallic length was 16 (14–18) cm and circumference 13 (11–15) cm, without flap loss or partial skin necrosis. Garaffa et al. reported radial artery forearm free flap reconstruction in 16 patients with bladder/cloacal exstrophy and micropenis-epispadias complex. One lost the distal third of the phallus to immediate postoperative arterial-anastomosis thrombosis. Almost all (93%) were fully satisfied with appearance and dimensions. Stricture and fistula at the native-neourethral junction were the commonest complications and were managed by revision. Of 12 patients receiving PPI, 11 achieved intercourse.

document_sections.heading: 9.3.2.2.5 Summary of evidence and recommendations for surgical treatment of congenital intrinsic penile shortness
document_sections.content: Given the range and complexity of interventions, the evidence summary says surgery should take place in high volume centres (LE 4). SLR, ventral phalloplasty, and suprapubic lipoplasty/liposuction/lipectomy objectively increase length (LE 3) but carry substantial complication rates (LE 3). TPR can provide satisfactory surgical and functional results in micropenis (LE 3). The recommendations specify performing AABP surgery in high volume centres (Strong); using SLR, ventral phalloplasty, and suprapubic lipoplasty/liposuction/lipectomy for lengthening (Weak); discussing their possible complications extensively (Strong); and using TPR to restore anatomy in congenital micropenis (Weak). The reference to AABP in this section’s high-volume-centre recommendation differs from its congenital-shortness evidence summary.

document_sections.heading: 9.3.2.3 Surgical treatment of acquired penile shortness
document_sections.content: The procedures discussed are penile prosthesis implantation (PPI), penile disassembly, corporal lengthening manoeuvres, and TPR after traumatic loss. Evidence and appropriateness differ between reconstructing lost anatomy and offering lengthening to patients seeking greater size.

document_sections.heading: 9.3.2.3.1 Penile prosthesis implantation (PPI)
document_sections.content: A direct link between PPI and increased length has not been established in ED without accompanying PD. Deveci et al. evaluated men receiving primary three-piece Alpha-1, Mentor, USA or two-piece Ambicor, AMS, Boston Scientific, USA implants for diabetes or RP. Most (72%) perceived shortening, but measured SPL did not change significantly. Another study implanted AMS 700 LGX in 45 patients with PD and no deformity or curvature < 30° or severe fibrosis/scarring; mean SPL changed from 13.1 ± 1.2 cm to 13.7 ± 1.1 cm at 6 months and 14.2 ± 1.2 cm at 12 months, with a significant further stretched-flaccid change between those follow-ups. In a prospective study excluding PD, erect length relative to pharmacologically induced baseline declined by 0.83 ± 0.25 cm at 6 weeks, 0.75 ± 0.20 cm at 6 months, and 0.74 ± 0.15 cm at one year after PPI. Another PD-excluding study reported median pharmacologically induced preoperative length of 14.25 ± 2 cm versus median post-prosthesis length of 13.5 ± 2.13 cm.

document_sections.heading: 9.3.2.3.2 Penile disassembly
document_sections.content: This proposed lengthening operation separates penile components and places autologous cartilage between the glans cap and corporal tips. Perovic et al. treated 19 patients with rib cartilage implantation followed by VED therapy, reporting SPL and erect-length gains of 3 cm and 3.1 cm, respectively. Surgical outcomes are poorly documented, and serious harm, including glans necrosis, may occur.

document_sections.heading: 9.3.2.3.3 Lengthening corporal manoeuvres
document_sections.content: The sliding technique (ST) with PPI was initially described in three patients in 2012 and then in a multicentre 28-patient series in 2015. It is used only for end-stage PD with severe shaft shortening. In the reported experience, 95% of men were satisfied with length gain, averaging 3.2 cm (range, 2.5-4 cm). Modified approaches include the modified sliding technique (MoST) and multiple slit technique (MuST). Egydio et al. treated 143 patients with PD-related or other shortening and narrowing using MoST or MuST; mean (range) gain was 3.1 (2-7) cm at median (range) follow-up of 9.7 (6-18) months.

document_sections.heading: 9.3.2.3.4 Total phallic reconstruction (TPR)
document_sections.content: A radial forearm free flap is the most commonly used TPR approach. Falcone et al. reported 10 patients reconstructed with RAFFF after traumatic loss. In 6, remaining urethral tissue permitted immediate anastomosis and neourethra formation; the others had complete avulsion, voided through a perineal urethrostomy, and required twostage urethroplasty. Two acute arterial-anastomosis thromboses were successfully managed by emergency exploration. One neourethral stricture and fistula needed revision. Everyone completing urethral repair could void and ejaculate through the phallus. After median follow-up of 51 months, all were satisfied with dimensions, appearance, and sensation. Six received PPI and could have penetrative intercourse; three needed revision, comprising 2 for infection and 1 for mechanical failure.

document_sections.heading: 9.3.2.3.5 Summary of evidence and recommendations for surgical treatment of acquired penile shortness
document_sections.content: The evidence summary states that PPI does not increase penile length (LE 3), support for penile disassembly and sliding manoeuvres is limited (LE 3), and TPR can produce satisfactory outcomes despite frequent postoperative complications (LE 3). Recommendations: do not recommend PPI, penile disassembly, or sliding technique as lengthening options for patients seeking increased length (Strong). Use TPR to restore anatomy in genetic males whose penis is inadequate because of traumatic loss (Weak).

document_sections.heading: 9.3.2.4 Penile girth enhancement
document_sections.content: Circumference enlargement is sought for cosmetic, confidence, or partner-related reasons. Techniques include injectable materials, fat transfer, grafts, scaffolds, and a subcutaneous implant; supporting evidence and safety vary.

document_sections.heading: 9.3.2.4.1 Penile Girth enhancement history
document_sections.content: Mean flaccid circumference is 9.31 cm (± 0.90 cm), compared with erect circumference of 11.66 ± 1.10 cm. Unlike lengthening, girth enlargement has no precise definition or indication in the cited literature or international guidelines. More men have recently sought it for confidence, cosmetic satisfaction, or partner satisfaction. Reports of techniques are relatively recent, and evidence for clinical use remains weak despite increasing requests and ethical concerns about operating on vulnerable patients.

document_sections.heading: 9.3.2.4.2 Injection therapy
document_sections.content: Injectable materials are categorised as autologous, biological, or synthetic. Autologous fat usually comes from liposuction. Biological materials include human or animal collagen and bacterial Hyaluronic acid. The synthetic list includes Poly-l-lactic acid (PLA), hydroxyethyl methacrylate, polyalkylimide hydrogel (PAAG), polymethylmethacrylate (PMMA), calcium hydroxyapatite (CHA), silicon, and paraffin. Table 9.5 groups fillers by origin.

document_sections.heading: Table 9.5: Origin of injectable filling materials
document_sections.content: The table groups Autologous fat tissue, Hyaluronic acid, and listed synthetic fillers by material origin.

document_sections.heading: 9.3.2.4.2.1 Soft tissue fillers (Hyaluronic acid and PMMA)
document_sections.content: Hyaluronic acid (HA) is widely used in plastic surgery. Penile use has grown because of biocompatibility and usually infrequent, mild, temporary adverse effects; crosslinked HA lasts longer. Reported girth increases range from 1.4 to 3.78 cm, with satisfaction of 78-100% and no reported severe adverse effects; Table S9.6 summarises studies. For PMMA, two studies reported an average circumference gain of 3.5 cm. Reported swelling and inflammation resolved within days, and investigators observed no migration pattern into adjacent tissue.

document_sections.heading: Poly-l-lactic acid
document_sections.content: Poly-l-lactic acid (PLA) stimulates fibroblast growth and collagen deposition. Reported penile-girth increase averages 1.2 to 2.4 cm. Treated patients had no reported complications apart from transient local pain and swelling.

document_sections.heading: 9.3.2.4.2.2 Other Fillers (silicone, paraffin)
document_sections.content: Patients or healthcare workers in many countries, especially in east Asia and east Europe, inject paraffin, silicone, or petroleum jelly (Vaseline) to increase girth. These foreign substances can trigger chronic granulomatous inflammation and sclerosing penile lipogranuloma, called paraffinoma or siliconoma according to the material. Consequences range from oedema or infection to Fournier’s gangrene. Excision of paraffinoma or siliconoma may require reconstructive surgery.

document_sections.heading: 9.3.2.4.3 Surgical therapy
document_sections.content: Surgical options for increasing circumference include harvested-fat injection, graft placement, tissue-engineered scaffolds, and a subcutaneous penile implant. Durability and complication data are limited for several approaches.

document_sections.heading: 9.3.2.4.3.1 Autologous fat injection
document_sections.content: This procedure removes lower-abdominal fat by liposuction and places the harvested tissue in the shaft. Retrospective studies report average circumference gains of 2 to 3.5 cm. They observed no statistically significant IIEF-score decrease or serious events such as abscess or deformity requiring another operation; more than 75% of patients reported satisfaction. Table S9.7 summarises the studies.

document_sections.heading: 9.3.2.4.3.2 Grafting procedures (albugineal and peri-cavernosal)
document_sections.content: Graft-based girth enlargement is considered experimental pending more rigorous multicentre complication and validated-outcome studies; Table S9.8 reviews it. In 69 patients receiving porcine dermal acellular matrix graft (InteXen; American Medical Systems, Minnetonka, MN, USA), reported girth gains at one year were 3.2 cm flaccid and 2.4 cm erect; 68 of 69 reported substantial satisfaction on Augmentation Phalloplasty Patient Selection and Satisfaction Inventory. Fibrosis occurred in up to 13%, and patients with fibrosis had mean length loss of 0.5 cm. Venous-graft techniques have encouraging early findings but need better-designed RCTs. Dermal fat grafts comprise deepithelialized dermis and subcutaneous fat and require a donor area of approximately 10 x 5 cm. Studies report girth gains of 1.67 to 2.3 cm, penile oedema up to 27%, painful erection up to 27%, and fibrosis-related curvature up to 9%; hypoesthesia, skin necrosis, and infection were not reported.

document_sections.heading: 9.3.2.4.3.3 Biodegradable scaffolds
document_sections.content: This approach cultures fibroblasts obtained from patients’ scrotal skin and dartos tissue on microporous biodegradable poly-lacti-co-glycolic acid (PLGA) scaffolds, which are implanted between Dartos and Buck’s fascia. A limited number of studies report girth increases up to 4.02 cm; Table S9.9 summarises the evidence.

document_sections.heading: 9.3.2.4.3.4 Subcutaneous penile implant (Penuma®)
document_sections.content: The recently approved Penuma® soft-silicone implant is positioned subcutaneously over 3/4 of the shaft and secured near the glans with polyester mesh. Studies report average circumference increases of 2 to 5 cm. Published complication rates, described as generally mild and temporary, are <5%, and the reported implant removal rate is 1%; both are characterised as relatively low.

document_sections.heading: 9.3.2.4.4 Summary of evidence and recommendations for penile girth enhancement
document_sections.content: The evidence summary finds limited benefit across girth-enlargement operations with differing outcomes and risks (LE 3). It lists HA, PLA, hydroxyethyl methacrylate, polyalkylamide hydrogel (PAAG), PMMA, and calcium hydroxyapatite as injectable materials (LE 3). Satisfaction with soft-tissue fillers, especially HA, PMMA, and PLA, is high (> 78%) (LE 3); aside from temporary local pain and swelling, complications were not reported in the cited filler patients (LE 3). Silicone, paraffin, and petroleum jelly (Vaseline) can cause effects from oedema and infection through Fournier’s gangrene (LE 3). Long-term evidence is insufficient for fat injection (LE 4), grafting with dermal acellular matrix, venous, or dermal fat grafts (LE 4), and biodegradable scaffolds or Penuma® (LE 4). Grafts are associated with high complication rates and low satisfaction (LE 3). Recommendations: counsel extensively about girth-procedure benefits and harms (Strong); do not use silicone, paraffin, or petroleum jelly (Vaseline) (Strong); use hyaluronic acid, soft tissue fillers, and autologous fat injection for girth enlargement (Weak), but do not use them in men with penile dysmorphic disorder (Strong); do not use grafts because they are experimental (Strong); and do not use biodegradable scaffolds or Penuma® for this purpose because they are experimental (Strong).

document_sections.heading: Figure 9.1: Management of short penile size
document_sections.content: The figure begins with a short-size complaint, medical and psychosexual history using instruments such as BAPS, assessment of common causes and other sexual problems including ED and PE, assessment for body dysmorphia, and focused examination documenting size and shape. It separates congenital intrinsic shortness, acquired intrinsic shortness, false shortness due to AABP, and normal size. Diagram labels include suspensory ligament release, ventral phalloplasty/scrotoplasty, and suprapubic lipoplasty for congenital intrinsic shortness (Weak); penile traction therapy (Weak); AABP management (Strong); psychosexual assessment (Strong); and total phallic reconstruction (Strong). It also labels penile lengthening with or without penile prothesis implantation and penile disassembly as not recommended (Weak). For the normal-size and BDD-assessment branches, the figure displays psychotherapy (Strong) and a separate group containing psychotherapy, penile traction therapy, suspensory ligament release, and soft-tissue fillers (each Weak), plus biodegradable scaffolds and subcutaneous penile implant labelled Experimental, Weak. The figure states that stretched length should be measured by both STT and BTT. Some figure labels differ from the preceding recommendation tables, notably total phallic reconstruction and the experimental scaffold and implant options; those differences should not be treated as a change to the tabulated recommendations.
